summary: For ages 6–7 (UK Y2, US Grade 2–3): recall and USE multiplication AND division facts for the 2, 5 and 10 tables, out of order and as fact families, built on structure rather than rote chanting. Derive 10s from place value, 5s as exactly half of the matching 10s fact, and 2s as doubles, so a forgotten fact can be re-derived. Teach division facts alongside multiplication (5×4=20 → 20÷5=4, 20÷4=5) and use commutativity so one learned fact delivers its partner. Connect the three tables to each other and to odd/even (the 2s = even numbers).
misconceptions: Being able to chant the table from the start but not recall a fact out of order — mistaking the chant for fluency.
Knowing the multiplication fact but not the corresponding division fact.
Treating 5×4 and 4×5 as separate facts to memorise (not using commutativity).
Confusing 'the 2 times table' with 'counting in 2s starting anywhere' — or muddling doubling with adding 2.
Not connecting 5s to 10s (missing that 5s are half the 10s), so each table is learned in isolation.

activities.title: Shade the table: derive the 5s from the 10s
steps: On a multiplication grid or hundred square, shade the 10s column (10, 20, 30, 40, 50…) and read them as place-value facts: 10×3 = 3 tens = 30.

Beside it, shade the 5s (5, 10, 15, 20, 25…) and line each 5s value up against the matching 10s value. On a multiplication grid this is the 5s column; on a hundred square the 5s fill two columns, the numbers ending in 5 and those ending in 0.
Notice and say aloud that each 5s value sits exactly halfway to the 10s value: 5×4 = 20 is half of 10×4 = 40.

Shade the 2s (on a multiplication grid, the 2s column; on a hundred square, every column ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8) and state that the answers in the 2s table are even numbers, and that 2×n is the double of n.
Pick one fact per table and write it as a derivation: '10×6 = 60, so 5×6 = 30 (half), and 2×6 = 12 (double of 6).'
Optionally, show the same facts as equal jumps on a number line (counting in 2s, 5s or 10s) to connect the shaded columns back to the skip-counting the child already knows.
activities.insight: The 2, 5 and 10 tables are a connected web, not three separate lists: 10s come from place value, 5s are half the matching 10s, 2s are doubles — so any fact can be rebuilt if forgotten.

activities.title: Four facts from one array: multiplication and its inverse
steps: Build or look at an array for one fact, e.g. 5 rows of 4 (= 20).
Write the two multiplication facts the array shows using commutativity: 5×4 = 20 and 4×5 = 20.
Write the two division facts from the same array: 20÷5 = 4 and 20÷4 = 5.
Repeat for several 2/5/10 facts, each time producing the full fact family of four facts from one picture.
Say why 20÷5 = 4 'has to be' true given 5×4 = 20 (sharing 20 into 5 equal rows gives 4).
activities.insight: One array holds a whole fact family; using commutativity and the inverse means learning one fact delivers its partners, so division facts are not extra memorising.

activities.title: Mixed quick-recall, out of order, with a derive-it fallback
steps: Once skip-counting is secure, answer facts asked OUT of sequence, mixing × and ÷: 5×3, 10×4, 2×7, then 20÷5, 30÷10, 14÷2.
For each, notice whether you knew it instantly or had to count, and say which.
On any fact you did not just know, use the derive-it route aloud: for a 5s fact, find the matching 10s fact and halve it; for a 2s fact, double the number.
Keep skip-counting available as a backup check, not as the main method.
activities.insight: Genuine fluency is recall out of order (including division), not a chant that only works from the start; when memory fails, a structured derivation recovers the fact.

activities.title: Trade-a-fact oral rehearsal
steps: Take turns with a partner: one asks a 2, 5 or 10 fact (× or ÷), the other answers, then they swap.
On a miss, the asker prompts the derivation: 'What's the ten fact? Now halve it' for 5s, or 'double it' for 2s.
Include inverse pairs deliberately, e.g. ask 5×6 then immediately 30÷5.
activities.insight: Spoken back-and-forth rehearsal gives extra meaningful retrieval and keeps the derive-it route verbal and quick.

checkQuestion: I'll ask some facts quickly — answer as fast as you can, and I'll watch whether you count to get there. 5 × 3? 10 × 4? 2 × 7? Now the division ones: 20 ÷ 5? 30 ÷ 10? 14 ÷ 2? (Watch whether recall is instant or reconstructed by skip-counting, and whether the division facts are as secure as the multiplication.)
checkAnswer: 15, 40, 14; 4, 3, 7 — answered from memory (or by very rapid skip-count), with the division facts as secure as the multiplication.
